terms.gloss: may I get up from the table?
evidence: Plaut. Ps. 296: postquam hercle istī ā mēnsā surgunt satis pōtī virī
terms.comment: Plautus says ā mēnsā surgere of guests getting up from the table; the request asks licet, as a child asks to go to the toilet or out to play, and the answer is Licet or Nōndum.

terms.gloss: get up from the table, leave the table

phrases.latin: postquam hercle istī ā mēnsā surgunt satis pōtī virī
phrases.english: ever since those fellows got up from the table well and truly drunk

phrases.latin: Licetne mihi ā mēnsā surgere? — Nōndum: prius holera comede.
phrases.english: May I get down? — Not yet: eat your vegetables first.
Yes, but wipe your mouth first.

sources: Lewis & Short: licet · Lewis & Short: surgo · Lewis & Short: mensa
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 28, 32.
